options.how: One difficulty for everyone with no selector at launch; the director argued separate modes would fragment the shared challenge.
Assist Mode toggles game speed down to 50%, infinite stamina, extra or infinite air dashes, dash assist and invincibility.

sources.note: Sekiro: FromSoftware on why there are no difficulty options
Celeste: granular Assist Mode options

options.how: A hidden rank shifts enemy aggression and damage as you take hits or die; the Professional setting locks it high so it never eases.
Opt-in God Mode starts at 20% damage resistance and adds 2% after each death up to 80%: adaptive, but visible and player-chosen.
The game never adjusts itself; Assist Mode changes only when the player toggles a setting, so the tuned challenge holds.

sources.note: Resident Evil 4 (2005): hidden dynamic difficulty
Hades: God Mode 20% resistance, +2% per death, cap 80%
Celeste: Assist options set manually by the player

options.how: Death leaves your souls and humanity at a bloodstain; touch it to recover them, but die again first and they are gone for good.
Death returns Madeline to the start of the screen instantly with infinite lives; the only cost is a few seconds.
On Ironman, one save is overwritten through every mission, so a soldier killed in combat is gone for good with no reload.

sources.note: Dark Souls: bloodstain recovery and loss on second death
Celeste: instant warp to the start of the screen on death
XCOM 2: Ironman single save, no do-overs

options.how: On Classic characters death drops half of each carried coin stack at a tombstone near the death spot; walk back to pick it up.
Losing the ship ends the run and deletes the save; there is no reload, so every jump and fight is final.

sources.note: Terraria: Classic drops coins at a tombstone, Mediumcore drops items, Hardcore deletes
FTL: permadeath, no second chances

options.how: Saving needs a typewriter and consumes one Ink Ribbon; ribbons are finite, so each save is a resource you choose to spend.
Autosaves trigger often after key moments and areas, so a death rarely costs more than a few minutes of play.

sources.note: Resident Evil: Ink Ribbons consumed by typewriter saves
God of War (2018): frequent autosave

options.how: Progress saves only at emergency phone stations, with no checkpoints; saving takes seconds and the alien can still find you mid-save.
The game autosaves about once a day with no manual slots; in Survival, dying without a resurrection item deletes the save.

sources.note: Alien: Isolation: manual save stations, no soft saves
Don't Starve: random-interval autosave, save deleted on death

options.how: Quicksave and quickload sit on single keys and work almost anywhere, so any fight can be retried from seconds earlier.
Automatic checkpoints land every few encounters and set pieces; there are no manual saves to manage, and death reloads the last one.
The game offers a save only after clearing a castle, fortress, ghost house or switch palace, so quitting mid-world loses the levels between.

sources.note: Half-Life: PC shooter with quicksave
Uncharted 2: Among Thieves: checkpoint-based progress
Super Mario World: saving after Game Over continues from the last save

options.how: Assist Mode doubles health to six, shows guide arrows, and returns Mario to safe ground in a bubble after a fall instead of killing him.
Housemarque deliberately left out difficulty settings; only aim assist strength can be raised, so everyone faces the same tuned loop.

sources.note: Super Mario Odyssey: Assist Mode gives six health, guide arrows and bubble rescue after falls
Returnal: director on the deliberate choice of no difficulty settings

options.how: Five difficulty levels per song plus 15 gameplay modifiers, such as faster song speed or no fail, let each player set the challenge.
Each rhythm game has one fixed tempo and timing window; there is no difficulty select, only optional medals and perfect runs.

sources.note: Beat Saber: 5 difficulty levels and 15 gameplay modifiers
Rhythm Heaven: Nintendo rhythm series with no difficulty settings

options.how: Each player toggles Smart Steering and Auto-Accelerate, and races run from 50cc to 200cc, so mixed-skill groups tune their own challenge.
No difficulty select by design; the studio bakes challenge into the run structure, and aim assist is the only lever players get.

sources.note: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe: Smart Steering and Auto-Accelerate per player; 50, 100, 150, Mirror and 200cc classes
Returnal: no difficulty settings, a deliberate decision by Housemarque

options.how: The AI Director tailors the frequency and ferocity of zombie attacks to how the team is doing, so pacing shifts every run.
Difficulty is one of four presets, Easy to Legendary, scaling enemy damage, health and shields; it holds steady while you play.

sources.note: Left 4 Dead: the Director tailors attacks to your performance
Halo: Combat Evolved: preset difficulty levels with enemy multipliers

options.how: After repeated deaths the game quietly adds an Aku Aku mask, slows hazards like the boulder, or turns a crate into a checkpoint.
Four fixed skill levels from Easy to Nightmare are set before play and change only on a level restart; nothing adapts to performance.

sources.note: Crash Bandicoot: Jason Rubin on Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (Aku Aku, slower boulder, crate continue points)
Quake: skill levels 0 Easy to 3 Nightmare; changes take effect on level restart

options.how: Catch-up logic quietly helps the trailing team, making late comebacks likely so blowouts stay rare and games stay close.
Both teams always share identical car stats and physics with no comeback help; matchmaking alone sets the level of challenge.

sources.note: NBA Jam: comeback logic for the trailing team
Rocket League: all cars have the same stats

options.how: Adaptive difficulty tunes enemy toughness and aim assist up or down behind the scenes according to how well you are doing.
The skill level chosen at the start fixes enemy damage and ammo for the run; the game never reacts to how you play.

sources.note: Max Payne: action shooter with adaptive difficulty
Doom: fixed skill levels

options.how: A death costs a life and restarts the level, or the midway point if reached; Game Over sends you back to the start of the world.
Heroes who die stay dead, and constant autosaving makes the loss final; you hire and level a replacement from the coach.

sources.note: Super Mario Bros.: lives, checkpoints and continuing from the start of the world
Darkest Dungeon: dead heroes stay dead, progress autosaves constantly

options.how: Dying drops part of your gold as floating money bags at the spot; reach them on the next try to win it back, or lose it.
Death leaves your whole inventory in a bag anyone can loot; you respawn with only a rock and a torch.
One hit kills you, and a key press restarts the floor instantly; the only cost is replaying a few seconds.

sources.note: Shovel Knight: gold dropped on death and recovered
Rust: survival game where death drops your inventory
Hotline Miami: instant restart after death

options.how: Many built-in accessibility options let players ease the platforming, while optional collectibles and Time Trials raise it for experts.
No difficulty select: FromSoftware gives every player the same tuned challenge so everyone shares one experience to discuss.

sources.note: Grapple Dog: play your way with optional collectibles, a Time Trial mode, or the many in-built accessibility options
Bloodborne: FromSoftware explains why Dark Souls, Bloodborne and Sekiro have no difficulty options

options.how: Item boxes deal items by distance and placement, so trailing racers get stronger tools to catch up and races stay close.
The chosen skill level fixes the challenge for the run; enemies never ease off or ramp up based on how well you are doing.

sources.note: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe: items are based on both distance and placement
Quake: fixed skill settings Easy, Normal, Hard, Nightmare

options.how: On normal difficulties manual saves, quicksaves and autosaves are all available, so any risky choice can be undone in seconds.
Progress autosaves constantly, so every action is permanent; a hero who dies stays dead with no reload to undo it.

sources.note: Fallout 4: on normal difficulty manual, quicksaving and autosaves are available (Survival restricts saving to beds)
Darkest Dungeon: progress autosaves constantly, so actions are permanent; dead heroes stay dead

options.how: Die to a player in the Wilderness and all but your 3 most valuable items drop for the killer (none if skulled), so gear is risked.
There are no lives; a defeat costs 100 Star Coins and restarts the current segment of the stage.

sources.note: Old School RuneScape: keep 3 most valuable items (0 when skulled); in the Wilderness non-protected items drop for the killer
Kirby and the Forgotten Land: no extra life system; defeat loses 100 Star Coins and restarts the segment
